Swiggy’s RTW is driven by 3 factors:

(1) Multiple past experiments with affordable food delivery: Swiggy POP (2017), PocketHero (2023) and 99 Store (2025). These learnings are invaluable on the demand side; to a great degree Swiggy chose Pune because of the demand density with college students & IT cos.

(2) Supply depth: Toing can draw from Swiggy’s 275k restaurant partners who are classified as monthly active. This is 100x of Ownly’s 2.3k restaurant partners (basis March ‘26 numbers). Swiggy is already going deep with select supply partners via Bolt & other formats. Toing is an extension of their core supply competency. 

(3) Commitment from management: Swiggy launched a standalone app for Toing. In the Q4 FY26 earnings call, founder Sriharsha said “Toing is intended to open up users who are, at best, infrequent on current food delivery.”

Execution needs to be flawless in the affordable food delivery space. It requires both demand density & deep supply partnerships in a given delivery polygon to make the unit economics work. 

Swiggy had successfully proven this model with POP pre-COVID by focusing on IT parks, dense residential neighborhoods & college accommodation blocks. 

Is there a risk of cannibalization of their core business? Possible yes!

Yet, Swiggy is making the non-consensus decision here to invest in Toing.

When Deepinder was asked about Toing in Q2 FY26, he said Zomato will "wait and watch" before introducing a separate app.

Swiggy has been the more innovative Food Delivery company in the country; ~1 in 5 orders come from New Initiatives (Bolt, 99 store, EatRight, Toing etc) as of Q4 FY26

It is just incredible to see listed companies tackle the Innovators Dilemma heads on - PB FinTech started PB Partners, Urban Company launched Insta Help & now Swiggy is building Toing. Founder led companies operate differently!

NoBroker offers many services:

(a) Packing & moving - launched in 2018 - 15 lakh+ shifts done

(b) Cleaning - launched in 2019 - 10 lakh+ cleanings done

(c) Painting - launched in 2019 - 5 lakh+ cleanings done

(d) Repairs (plumbing, carpentry & electrical works) - launched in 2020

(e) Interior design - launched in 2022 - 30k+ homes delivered

For NoBroker, this is logical extension to its core home purchase & rental marketplace - these services are always required alongside the platform transaction. 

Of course, this is the 1st time NoBroker will be providing services to humans - all the other services are for the home, appliances or fixtures.

I’ve been following the Quick Services trendline for over 18 months now.

Quick has become the baseline expectation. I remain skeptical - I sense this is artificial supply led demand creation versus true demand pull (outside of very specific user archetypes which one finds in metros).

Category expansion has become the default. Each category sees entry by one incumbent & at least one new funded startup. 

Most will die. Few winners will emerge because of the structural advantage of Economies of Scope i.e. profitability maths works out when you offer multiple service categories to the acquired & retained user (UC has proven this as a public company for its core India business).

➡️But, for now, it feels like a royal rumble where everyone is taking on everyone (until the music & funding stops).

The media coverage of Turtlemint’s IPO missed a key nuance about Blume Venture’s holdings in the company.

The media correctly states that Blume is sitting on a meagre 1.63x gain from Fund 1X

But, this begs the question - WTF is Fund 1X?

In Blume’s Omega Files disclosure in 2024, they highlighted that Fund 1X was a continuity vehicle which bought the top positions of Blume Fund 1A (including Turtlemint) at FMV.

Per Turtlemint’s RHP filings, on 25th Feb 2021, Blume 1X bought ₹54 crore worth of shares from Blume 1A which generated a 19.2x return on the cumulative ₹2.82 crore capital invested.

Blume 1X invested further capital into Turtlemint at a valuation higher than the IPO price - which is why Blume’s blended return from Turtlemint is 1.63x

In reality, Blume has generated a 36.7x return on Turtlemint (.e. 39.5% XIRR) for LPs who held on to their Fund 1A investment through Fund 1X

My reason for posting this is because I too was surprised to see Blume 1X have a lower MOIC than Nexus IV in the RHP filings. 

Most of us don’t fully understand Continuity vehicles (e.g. Blume Fund 1X) therefore it is important to distinguish original cost from transferred cost.

On an original cost basis, Turtlemint would be a 1x fund return for Blume 1+1A (total corpus of ~₹120 crore) 😇

Much as I would love to write a post about Turtlemint and the POSP insurance business, I'm afraid I can't since I know a bit too much about the industry (since Verak's acquirer InsuranceDekho was primarily a POSP business).

However, what I can share is that the Turtlemint founders are held in high regard by their peers & industry insiders  😃 

To a great degree, they were pioneers in driving adoption of the POSP model

Manu invested ~₹55 crore into Innovist across all 6 rounds - he concentrated 30% of his 1st VC fund into a single company. Yesterday, his calculated risk was richly rewarded:

L'Oreal has announced its intent to acquire a majority stake in Innovist at an estimated ~₹3,300 crore to ₹4,100 crore valuation.

What does this mean for Manu? At the top end of the spectrum:

Sauce VC’s 13.39% stake is worth ₹550 crore i.e. an 10x return on the ₹50 crore invested.

What makes it more remarkable is that the 10x is before factoring an additional ₹40 crore of secondary sales done.

But, Sauce VC invested via 2 vehicles - Fund I and Continuity Fund I - into Innovist:

For the ₹60 crore Fund I, Innovist is a 26x return & therefore an 8x fund return (by itself) 🤯

Innovist will generate ₹480 crore of distributions (via 10.97% ownership & ₹32 crore of past realized sales) on ₹26 crore invested from Fund I.

I’ve always admired Manu & Sauce VC’s approach to Consumer investing; there are 3 key principles which I pointed out earlier this yr as well:

(1) Concentration - 30% of Fund I went into a top company; Manu & team typically do 9-10 investments per fund.

(2) Liquidity/taking chips off the table - Sauce VC had already sold ~₹42 crore of secondaries i.e. almost recovered the entire ₹50 crore invested prior to this acquisition.

(3) Power Law works in Consumer - look at Innovist, it has returned the fund 8 times over

Basis public information, Sauce VC Fund I should be tracking at 14x i.e. over ₹840 crore of holdings generated in ~7 years from a ₹60 crore capital base 🤯

Anyone who says Consumer in India cannot support venture scale outcomes needs to study Sauce’s playbook.

Full credit to Manu, Yash & team Sauce VC for picking winners and to the incredible founders they have partnered with like Innovist, The Whole Truth, XYXX & many others.

AI is not replacing jobs. There is a fundamental difference between a collection of tasks & a job.

Job = U { Tasks, Judgment, Relationships, Context, Ownership}

Few jobs are truly at risk of replacement by AI - these involve more deterministic IO (Input Output) execution e.g. data entry, QA, CS etc.

Most jobs are resilient because:

(1) Human principals (business owners) always seek to assign responsibility & blame to a human agent.

(2) Deals get done not because of outbound spam but because of years of nurturing a relationship (showing up at conferences, events, meet-ups)

(3) The physical world is messy AF. Humans read non-verbal & subtle cues which are only possible via in-person interactions.

The midwits are right - AI is taking over tasks. In fact, if AI hasn’t taken over tasks for you then you’re doing something very wrong.

If tasks are automated & workflows are changing, jobs won’t be lost. In fact, to manage the messy transition, humans will be more in demand than ever before.

The data from Foundation Labs itself points to this (watch to the end of this rant)

The Whimsical mind map which I created can be found via the link here:

https://t.co/kKsGnGXC05

In the sprit of transparency, I gave ChatGPT a long mental dump of my thoughts on this topic & worked with it to develop the framework. Post which, I used Whimsical AI to generate the flowchart.

Btw, I am also 100% guilty of stating that AI would replace the VC Analyst role - I think it has changed what an Analyst now means for the firm.

An IIMA classroom project raised $1m today to offer authentic, affordable & domestically produced Ramen.

Nishank and Akhil observed that roadside vendors in Ahmedabad selling Korean ramen were quite successful. This led to an insight - if a snack is now available as street food, it has deep cultural penetration.

Customer feedback revealed that street ramen felt like ramen flavored masala noodles. The authentic alternatives were cup noodles which felt too processed or imported brands which are quite expensive (₹120 per packet).

This was their “Maggi Moment” - customers needed a semi-prepared packet which felt DIY but didn’t involve too much cooking (adding noodles + water + veggies).

The duo received a ₹14 Lakh grant from IIMA which allowed them to iterate for several months on the flavor profile by running a pop-up on campus. Once they locked this in, they began selling on Amazon & Flipkart - the reception was incredible - they made their first ₹8 Lakhs in sales.

In a few weeks, they had a term sheet for a Pre-Seed round from India Quotient, Titan Capital, IIMA Ventures and us (DeVC).

Gimi Michi is on absolute 🔥 - sales have grown x25 in the 8 months since our investment and the growth rate even now holds steady at 50% MoM. Gimi was selling ₹5 Lakh per month when we invested, it has scaled to ₹1.2 crore per month now 🤯

Today, Gimi Michi announced its total $1m Seed funding led by India Quotient. DeVC is doubling down on our partnership with Nishank and Akhil by adding more capital as part of this round.

K-Culture continues its India takeover - we saw this with Boba Bhai (an early DeVC investment), public data from Nykaa suggests K-Beauty is growing 58% YoY and India is the 7th largest global market for K-Pop steaming.

Gimi Michi is riding a clear tailwind where customers are voting with their wallet.

The brand has an interesting ₹40-50 per packet price point - roughly 1.5x the cost of Maggi (per gram) but 1/3rd the cost of imported Ramen alternatives.

India’s Ramen market is expected to cross $ 1bn in the next 10 yrs. Per Blinkit data, 34% of noodles sold on Quick Commerce are Korean variants (up 30x over the course of 2 yrs)

I can never find any stock of their Hot Chicken, Crazy Cheesy or Korean Spicy variants in our office pantry - they are consumed by my colleagues faster than our facilities team can place orders 😂

You can order Gimi Michi via their website or from any E-Commerce or QC app directly to your doorstep - I can promise you will enjoy the authentic Korean Ramen taste 😇

I've met a dozen new VC fund managers in India this yr. One consistent theme across these meetings:

Their 1st hire is an "AI tinkerer" who is tasked with setting up an AI native system for the fund:

* CRM automations
* Mining & scraping pipeline
* Ops workflows

I have also observed that established funds have also begun actively hiring for this type of role.

Every fund manager has realized that several founder patterns can codified as external signals which are interpreted by LLMs

The tech renaissance come to VC world nearly 20 yrs after the HFT explosion hit the public markets.

As private markets deepen (esp. in India), Tech becomes a core competency for an investment institution.

Hence, you will see more fund managers hire for this skill set - which aligns with what has already taken place in the public markets.

PS: 15 months ago, I was laughed out of internal & external rooms when I was pushing for AI led automations.

I now receive (at least) one serious message daily asking to exchange notes about building an AI native Fund OS.

Unfortunately, it is a bit like asking RenTech to tell you about their algos - everyone has to codify their own secret sauce; we've been through this painful but rewarding journey.

UC is saving ~₹35 crore per annum by using AI

Per UC’s Q4 FY26 filings, 55% of partner support queries are handled by AI. 

This has reduced the support cost per partner visit down from ~₹40 to ₹31.5 per order.

Voice AI plays a major role at UC in onboarding new partners, providing real-time query resolution during fixing and doing multi-way calls to coordinate visits.

Last month, Raghav Chandra, Co-Founder & CPTO of UC, demoed their AI assistant on stage at Mumbai Tech Week. 

He showed how UC’s AI assistant helped a service professional resolve a technical doubt while at the client’s home.

Their AI deployment scale is already meaningful:
1️⃣ 2.35 crore in-service job images processed Q4 FY26
2️⃣ 5 lakh call minutes handled in Q4 FY26
3️⃣ 100% of in-service images audited against SOPs in real time

Outside of partner enablement, UC is also using AI to improve its customer experience - placing filter reminder calls for Native, visualization of interiors in UC Revamp and much more.

➡️ For UC, the ₹35 crore of annualized savings represents a whopping 25% of the adjusted EBITDA figure in their core India biz. This is material & they are just getting started.

I first met Aadit & KV on 6th January 2021 during our YC W21 office hours.

KiranaKart was delivering in a small radius within Bandra offering pick-ups from nearby kirana stores.

I was 20 kms away from their house but I couldn’t place an order.

One of our YC W21 batchmates told me: “Those Kirana dudes will get cooked by competition.”

5.5 yrs later, KiranaKart (now Zepto) is ready to IPO after filings its UDRHP. This is the fastest time from founding to IPO in our country in recent years.

Zepto fulfilled 64 crore orders in FY26 which translates to 23 Lakh orders per day in Q4 FY26🤯

Quick Comm is an operationally intensive biz & requires tuning multiple levers on the path to profitability (which has been demonstrated in this industry).

Zepto is making huge progress on this pathway to profitability:

(1) Ad revenue has grown 33x from ₹49 crore in FY24 to ₹1636 crore in FY26

(2) Orders per day (OPD) per store has increased 60% from 1325 in Q1 FY24 to 2140 in Q4 FY26

(3) Burn per order has reduced 50% from ₹93.4 in Q1 FY24 to ₹42 in Q4 FY26

Zepto’s thesis was always the “densification flywheel” i.e. low AOV with high frequency results in higher density of orders per dark store. Higher order volume for given CAPEX reduces the fixed cost per order.

Zepto has intentionally focused on metro cities where this density can be built.

A lot of armchair critics ask “can this $ 7bn valuation private company become $ 10bn someday?”

The only thing I’ve seen Aadit & KV do is to execute relentlessly - raise $ 2.3bn, hire 18.3k staff and build a brand which is synonymous with the purple color in metro cities.

At every juncture, I’ve people criticize these two founders - the need for quick commerce (2021), how grocery alone won’t cut it (2022), why 10 mins is unsustainable (2023), the tough work culture (2024) & now profitability.

➡️It is incredible to have seen this company go from a pilot in Bandra to being omnipresent across some cities - we all see the Zepto purple zip past us on a daily basis!

SNITCH has been a 17 year rollercoaster for Siddharth Dungarwal

> Opened a cloth retail store in 2009 (still in college)

> Seatback: got stuck with ₹25L inventory

> Snitch 2.0 (2012 to 2019) was a B2B fashion house

> COVID was the reset; “fast fashion needs a supply chain” was his reflection 

> Snitch 3.0 was a D2C brand

> Bootstrapped to ~₹100 cr of revenue then raised VC money 

> Grew 9x in 3 years to ₹900 crore 🤯

Here’s how SNITCH got started ⤵️

What lessons does Sid have for D2C founders?

Sid did an incredible interview with Ganesh from Think School approx. 2 years ago where he shared some lessons:

(1) Grow via website sales initially - first party data is valuable in the early days of brand creation; lets you identify which pin codes your customers are coming from!

(2) Control your supply chain: Snitch’s concept to store loop is < 1 month whereas traditional fashion houses take 6+ months. Fashion must be “Fast” and SNITCH’s contract manufacturers are “partners” and not “vendors”

(3) Inventory discipline: Fast fashion should ideally have 45–60 days inventory

(4) Dead stock (above 365 days) should be sub 4%

(5) Going offline is required but target rent to revenue target of 10–12% (in steady state)

Sid has stuck to these principles - offline stores opened only once the brand had crossed ₹100 crore of Sales (FY23) and website remains a large part of the overall business.

SNITCH began as a Sid’s college hustle but has transformed into his life’s work almost 17 years later.

He has proven that with patience - it is possible to build a ₹100 crore D2C brand while being fully bootstrapped - I believe his background in contract manufacturing was a big edge.

➡️SNITCH  thrives in the Fast Fashion industry because it has mastered being “Fast” - getting from concept to store in weeks and not months!

Lakmé was born in 1952 because South Delhi aunties protested in front of PM Nehru

Sounds absurd but there was a real problem: Post independence, our Govt restricted the import of non-essential products which included cosmetics to conserve our limited FOREX reserves.

Therefore, foreign products such as Hazeline Snow, Pond’s and Lux were no longer available on shelves.

Apart from Afghan Snow (Patanwala), there were few domestic alternatives. the South Delhi aunties had every right to protest 😆

The Lakmé story involves Independence, France, Tata Group & HUL ⤵️

3️⃣ Growth of Lakmé under HUL

As part of HUL, Lakmé faced ferocious competition from international players L'Oréal in the post Liberalization

HUL doesn’t break out Lakmé numbers specifically, the brand is estimated to do ₹4,000+ crore in Sales -

Therefore, if you apply a conservative 5x Sales multiple - Lakmé would be a ₹20,000 crore brand - making this is a 125x return before factoring in CAPEX & working capital infusions over the years 🤑

A few decisions stood out:

(a) Launch of Lakmé Fashion Week (LFW) in 2000 which runs twice a year now

(b) Expansion of Lakmé Salons (the Lakmé  Lever entity does ₹375 crore in Revenue as a franchise operator)

(c) Focus on the modern Indian woman with ranges like Lakmé Eyeconic and 9to5

For the past decade, Lakmé has also also faced a lot of competition from startup BPC brands which have crossed the ₹100 crore revenue mark (e.g. Dot & Key, WishCare, Minimalist etc)

To consolidate the market like it did 30 yrs ago, HUL paid ₹2500+ crore to buy 90% of The Minimalist. I expect HUL to do several such transactions

Lakmé’s name itself captures the contradiction of post-Independence India.

The brand drew inspiration from Lakshmi, the goddess of beauty and prosperity - but had to adopt a French accent to appeal to an elite consumer who associated beauty with the West.

70 years later, that tension still defines Indian consumption: local roots but global taste.

➡️ The origin story of Lakmé was covered in “The Tata Group” - a fascinating book written by Dr Shashank Shah - I’ve thoroughly enjoyed reading this book & would highly recommend you pick up a copy

1.2 crore Indians bought at least one K-Beauty product last year

India’s obsession with Korea has extended to beauty products as well

> Expected to grow 4x in India over the next 5 yrs to ₹14,000 crore in annual Sales

> 58% YoY growth on Nykaa Beauty (x2 faster than platform average of 27%)

> 25% CAGR in India (also x2 faster than industry average of 11%)

Despite this growth, K-Beauty is less than 5% of the overall BPC market in India

Data tells us that this theme has a long runway ahead ⤵️

Nykaa launched 27 K-Beauty brands in FY26

This represents more than 10% of the ~200 brands which Nykaa added in FY26 - clearly indicating this category has serious tailwinds.

the FY26 launches cover the full BPC routine:

(1) Derma via Aestura, Illiyoon & Medicube
(2) Skincare via Anua, Dr Althea, Torriden & Mixsoon
(3) Haircare via RYO & Mise-en-scène
(4) Gen Z makeup via Fwee
(5) Premium / vegan skincare via d’Alba
(6) Masks / treatment formats via Biodance

For the first time, Nykaa allocated time to discuss K-Beauty during the earnings call to highlight the global trend & how Nykaa had built the sourcing, category & assortment muscle to ride this wave.

K-beauty is not new to India

Innisfree entered India in 2013. Nykaa launched K-Beauty in 2016. 

But, it took 10 yrs for the breakout to appear in FY26

As India assimilates more aspects of Korean culture (food, pop music & drama TV shows), the demand for K-Beauty products will only continue to rise.

➡️The winners in K-Beauty will localize the Korean beauty playbook for Indian skin, climate, price points and distribution channels.

This wave will be no different from previous ones such as men's grooming, toxin-free, SPF based formulations and active ingredients.

Many partners have realized that 90% of the leg work can be done using AI.

This makes the prospect of starting up more alluring - esp. since they've all made some money from IPOs & are tired of doing team management, committee meetings and social pleasantries 

But, the remaining 10% of work (which is 90% of the job) still needs founder DNA to get out into the field, hustle hard & pursue opportunities.

For some, the allure of building an institution in a post AI era is worth the fees v/s carry trade-off.

But, for each of them who choose this path, they still go up against their former partners whom they have inadvertently empowered by freeing up more seats at the table.

IMHO, very good for the ecosystem - more funds means more cheque writers who will lead rounds (which is most needed in our country).

Balaji Wafers is the anti-thesis of India’s consumption narrative.

Started in 1984 as a potato wafers brand in Rajkot, Balaji is now a ₹6,500 crore revenue business with ~12% share of India’s salty snacks market.

The market narrative says: health-first, premiumization & pan-India distribution.

Balaji did exactly the opposite:

> Affordable instead of Premium
> Tasty instead of Healthy
> Regional density before Pan-India expansion

Due to this strategy, Balaji has grown 22.5% CAGR from FY20 to FY25 - much faster than the industry average of 15% CAGR

The Balaji story holds one key lesson ⤵️

The lesson is: Be Yourself (whatever the cost)

Balaji has done 3 things differently from competition:

1️⃣ More grammage at same price

Balaji’s proposition remains simple: “More product for the same ₹10”

Their ₹10 salted chips pack had 35g v/s Lay’s 23g 

2️⃣ Consumer trust over short-term margin

During FY22, revenue grew 36%, but profit almost disappeared.

PAT fell to ~₹7 Cr as material costs shot up to 86%+ of revenue.

Chandubhai Virani put it: “If people trust you, the business will grow.”

3️⃣Preserve Taste above all else

The urban narrative says snacks are moving to millet, protein, baked, low-calorie, better-for-you formats.

Balaji gives its ICP what they really want - a tasty, filling & affordable snack at the ₹5 and ₹10 price point.

Last yr was an inflection point for Balaji

Last yr, 42 yr Balaji raised its 1st external funding round (₹3,500 crore) from PE firm General Atlantic

The company has a 4.5 Lakh strong kirana distribution network which it has patiently built one state at a time.

The 2nd generation has slowly taken over the business: expanding from 10 to 100 SKUs, opening more automated plants in new states and doubling the distributor count.

➡️Balaji is the anti-thesis of our consumption narrative: It has always been a volume, value and regional distribution story.

My grandfather bought the original Titan Quartz Classique 289-06 on the very first day Titan opened its Mumbai store in 1990.

He kept the watch in mint condition for 35 years until he gifted it to me on my 27th birthday https://t.co/wbf9abw5bG

The reason why I got it on my 27th birthday is that his parents gifted him his first watch when he was aged 27 (back in 1964)

It is an incredible piece of Indian engineering and history which I'm very proud to wear every alternate day of the week.

If you're watching "Made In India: A Titan Story" on Amazon Prime, then you should also read the book "Titan" by Vinay Kamath.

My grandfather encouraged me to read it 2 yrs ago - I couldn't understand why (since he never bought the Titan stock)

But, my appreciation for the Titan watch he gifted me would be nowhere near what it is today.

Anushka Sharma is the most recent celebrity to invest in Abhishek Ganguly’s new company

Agilitas Sports has a star-studded list of athletes & celebrities who are not just passive cheque-writers.

Celebrity endorsements in India are now becoming ownership-led

Let us look at the list for Agilitas⤵️

The star studded cap table includes:
(1) Virat Kohli -  invested ₹40 crore for ~1.9%
Agilitas acquired Kohli’s brand One8 and is repositioning it as a homegrown Indian performance sportswear brand.

(2) Anushka Sharma - invested ₹3.78 crore for ~0.2%
Co-developing One8 Yoga, a yoga-wear line under the One8 franchise.

(3) Yuvraj Singh invested ₹5 crore for ~0.5%
He is the brand ambassador of Lotto India (Agilitas Sports owns this license now); he co-invested alongside Virat.

(4) Abhishek Sharma invested  ₹1 crore for <0.1%
SRH cricketer and one of the faces for Lotto India’s launch.

(5) Saurav Ghosal invested ₹1.5 Cr for <0.1%
India’s most decorated squash player. He has joined Agilitas as Director – High Performance Sports, bringing athlete credibility into product/R&D

(6) Hardevinder Singh Sandhu invested  ₹4 crore for ~0.4%
No public brand-collaboration announcement here; but I believe one might come along soon

Abhishek is not an ordinary brand founder. He scaled Puma India from ₹20 crore to ~₹3,900 crore in sales during his 18-year stint

He also convinced Virat to walk away from a ₹300 crore renewal contract for One8 with Puma India and instead invest ₹40 crore  into Agilitas.

The key learning from Agilitas is simple: Celebrity endorsements are transactional. Celebrity ownership, if structured correctly, can be deeper & more meaningful.

Agilitas is trying to combine celebrity equity, brand IP, manufacturing and distribution under one roof.

Agilitas raised an additional ₹225 crore in funding last week - ₹200 crore from Nexus Venture Partners and ₹25 crore from Rainmatter

If Abhishek Ganguly pulls this off, Agilitas could become one of India’s most consequential consumer-brand platforms in India. It would provide the template for future celebrity-operator partnerships to create brands.

Grandma stood up from the bed for the 1st time today approx. 45 days after her surgery

We still have a long journey ahead for her to stand unassisted and even longer (if at all) for her to walk again

When I met her in hospital, I promised her that we would all put in effort - she was afraid & didn't want to even try standing.

So I promised her, I wouldn't drink a single cup of coffee (which she knows I love) until she can walk again

If that means no coffee ever again, it is totally something I am okay with.

I told her: "We're all in" and after 4 long weeks of physio, this morning, it was a real delight to see standing (even if it was for 15 seconds with help)

China built ‘Super Apps”. India is building “Super Companies”

In the late 2010s, it seemed like India would go down the same Super Apps route as China - every investor was looking for “India’s WeChat”

WhatsApp could never become WeChat for India. Paytm tried doing so with moderate success. Tata Neu burnt a ₹17000 crore hole trying to be everything to everyone.

In recent years, every major consumer internet platform in India has built a constellation of apps versus a Super App.

One super company with many focused apps and cross-app linkages (shared login, address & preferences) to improve customer experience. 

Pundits argued that crowded apps represented Indian bazaars therefore Super Apps would work in India 😂

The reason why Super Companies emerged in India is because our internet platforms BOUGHT and did not always BUILD (like China):

(a) Swiggy bought Dineout and Supr Daily (latter which led to Instamart)

(b) Zomato bought Grofers which became Blinkit

(c) Flipkart bought PhonePe (pre-launch) and ClearTrip

Each acquisition brought with it a team, tech stack & customer base which is a difficult M&A integration challenge.

➡️Indian internet platforms are starting to look like our legacy conglomerates - a shared back-end but a fragmented front-end to cater to disparate India.

Zara’s growth engine in India has stalled.

Revenue has been stuck around ₹2,750 crore for the past 3 yrs

Meanwhile, PAT is down 23% from ₹265 crore in FY23 to ₹205 crore in FY26.

At the same time, Trent (Tata Group) has reduced its ownership in Zara India from 49% to 20% in the past 2 yrs.

On the other hand, Zara’s parent Inditex remains bullish on India - it now owns 80% of Zara India and launched Bershka in India directly outside the Tata JV

So, what exactly is happening here? ⤵️

3️⃣ Zara is stuck in the Messy Middle of Fashion

At the top end, affluent consumers are trading up into to luxury, Indian designers, Massimo Dutti & other aspirational brands.

At the bottom end, value fashion has exploded: Zudio, Yousta, Style Up, Max Fashion, Reliance Trends, Myntra/Ajio private labels and online trend-first brands.

And in the middle, Zara has stiff competition from H&M, Uniqlo, Mango, Gap, Forever 21 and now Bershka.

So Zara is being attacked from both sides:

(a) Price: Too expensive for value fashion. Not premium enough for true luxury/status fashion.

(b) Selection: And no longer uniquely fast enough versus online trend discovery.

Zara has been stuck in the “messy middle” of Fashion for the past few yrs.

I’ve seen this first hand - we use to be a Zara household but we’re now a UNIQLO heavy household ever since they launched stores in India.

Outside of UNIQLO, Zara faces competition from 100s of upstart consumer brands which are slicing the market in different ways - age, formats, channels, designs, speed & much more.

The positive sign here is: Zara might have slowed down, but Zara’s owner Inditex remains bullish on India’s fashion market - it has increased ownership in Zara India & launched Bershka.

Now the only Zara I hear of from my friends is Zara Larsson 😂

1️⃣ Zara went through hyper growth from FY15 to FY20

Between FY15 and FY20, Zara India revenue grew from ~₹704 crore to ~₹1,571 crore i.e. 2.2x growth in 5 years (~17% CAGR.)

But this was not store-led growth. Zara already had 16 stores in FY15. By FY22, it had only 21 stores.

The pre-COVID boom was driven by store productivity where the brand  rode 3 big India trends:

(a) Premium mall-led consumption

(b) Young urban consumers wanting global fashion

(c) India’s growing fascination with global brands

In simple terms: Zara became the default “aspirational & global” fashion brand for the urban Indian.

2️⃣ Then, came the COVID slump, rebound & plateau:

FY21 was ugly: revenue fell and Zara India made a loss. Then came revenge shopping.

Revenue jumped to ~₹1,815 crore in FY22 and ~₹2,554 crore in FY23.

But after that, growth has stalled for the past 3 yrs.

The clearest symbol of this slowdown was Zara shutting its iconic South Bombay Flora Fountain store in Feb 2025. The store was huge, expensive, and reportedly had ~₹30 crore annual rent.

As of FY26, Zara still has 22 stores in India (flat for the past 5 yrs).

My hypothesis: The root cause is not fewer store openings. Rather it is that India’s fashion market has structurally changed.

(3) Supply friendly terms in a supply constrained market

Imagine charging 0 commission from a partner - this is the reality of the at-home salon services industry.

There are few professionals who will give up the comfort of working in an AC salon for navigating crowded, hot or rainy streets to make home appointments.

Typically, platforms like UC charge 25% commission for various home services - the highest slab of YM is lower!

There are several reasons why YM has to do this - supply leakage, competition, non-availability of skilled labor etc

In fact, like UC, YM has a mandatory 15-day training programme covering SOPs, hygiene standards and BWSSC certification (a Govt approved program)

Like L’Oréal & Lakmé which have their own academies for further study - YM invests in personality development, advanced makeup training & other skills.

In addition to training, YM provides accident & health insurance to its partners at a small cost.

If partners are expecting a child - YM drops commission to 0% to help their partners save money towards pregnancy related expenses

This is a supply dominated market where availability is constrained and addition of new supply takes a long time due to the upskilling journey

This week, Yes Madam raised its maiden funding round of ₹50 crore from Info Edge Ventures at a ₹750 crore valuation.

This company carries an important lesson for founders operating in irrationally competitive markets.

Sometimes, you just have to survive the chaos in order to thrive in the calmness.

Mayank, Aditya & team YM have been incredibly resilient through this 9+ yr journey and have built a great franchise.

They might face short-term competition from the Quick Services players (e.g. Dazzl, Snabbit, Pronto etc).

➡️However, their core insight from 2017 remains - speed might get you the first order & funding but trust, hygiene & consistency will give you repeat behavior.

(1) Yes Madam survived long enough to become a Product company

During 2017-2018 there were over a dozen funded at-home salon companies

A few got acquired e.g. AtHomeDiva by Quikr, VanityCube by VLCC, StayGlad also by Quikr. Most shut down.

Only Yes Madam (YM) & Urban Clap (now called UC) remained - during this highly competitive period, Yes Madam kept its burn in check & lived through COVID.

Think about your salon experience: An expensive product is used during the treatment. Both the professional & the owner try to cross-sell you some products lying on their shelves during the billing process.

During COVID, the founders realized that their business model which relied on Services only was not sufficient - they needed to start selling products & capture the high margins which exist in BPC products.

Therefore, YM spent time creating its own white label kits & products.

Customers are free to choose between using YM’s own product or their own products (in which case they are only charged for services)

Despite this, you will notice that the majority of YM’s operating revenue comes from sale of Goods.

This reinforces the core insight - customers have to trust the products being used by at-home professionals

(2) Improved Gross Margins on Products

Revenue from sale of goods has grown 3.5x in the past 3 yrs and remains > 50% of the Operating Revenue

In the same time (FY22 to FY24), the gross margin earned from these goods has almost doubled from 19% to 37%

The YM financials extracted from TRACXN clearly show how Economies of Scale are working in favour of the company

The GM on these goods (37%) is MUCH higher than the GM which the company earns on Services (which I believe is closer to 15% since booking revenue is split with the partner)

Therefore, as YM scales up, a larger share of its PAT will be driven by the sale of consumables which are used by its service professionals.

This supports their supply friendly pricing model:

In 2016, a routine at-home salon appointment went horribly wrong. 

Yukti & Garima suffered from allergic reactions after a beautician used expired products

Yukti’s husband Mayank was enraged - this is how Yes Madam was born

Their core insight: Customers wanted salon-like treatments at home but could not trust the professional, hygiene standards or products being used.

9 yrs later, Mayank & his younger brother Aditya have built a profitable ₹100 crore revenue business while being bootstrapped.

Here’s how they survived a category where most funded players disappeared ⤵️
